title: Arrhenius Equation

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Chemical Kinetics

explanation: The Arrhenius equation describes how the rate constant of a reaction depends on temperature and activation energy. As temperature increases, more molecules have enough kinetic energy to overcome the activation energy barrier, so k (and therefore the reaction rate) increases — this is the mathematical explanation for why reactions generally speed up with heating. A catalyst works by providing an alternative pathway with a LOWER activation energy, increasing k without needing a temperature change.

variables.meaning: Pre-exponential (frequency) factor — related to collision frequency and orientation

resultUnit: Same unit as the rate constant k

workedExample.scenario: Comparing the same reaction at two temperatures illustrates the equation's practical use: the two-temperature form ln(k₂/k₁) = −(Ea/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) lets Ea be calculated from rate constants measured at two different temperatures.
workedExample.result: Solving for Ea gives the activation energy from experimental k values at T₁ and T₂

commonMistakes: Forgetting T must be in Kelvin.
Assuming a catalyst changes A significantly rather than its real effect: providing a lower-Ea pathway.
genZNote: The Arrhenius equation is why 'just heat it up' is basically chemistry's universal cheat code for faster reactions — more molecules clear the activation energy bar.
